Handovers are where reasoning pours out

Analysislowob research

By lowob · 1 October 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

In short: Reasons leak from organisations all the time. At handovers they pour out, all at once, on a date everyone knows in advance. The standard handover transfers files, logins and a status list, which is what was already written down, and loses the reasoning, which was not. A five-part pack started four weeks before departure keeps it: extracted decisions, open threads, relationships, a graveyard of abandoned approaches, and a question log for the first 90 days. For an organisation with no judgment record, it is the cheapest place to start one.

Key points

  • A standard handover transfers what is already written down and loses what is not, which is the part that mattered.
  • Group research shows information held by only one person is the least likely to be raised or recorded, so reasoning does not transfer by proximity.
  • Decision records exist to let later joiners understand "why the system is constructed in the way that it is"; a handover is the moment that need becomes urgent.
  • Extract the outgoing person's ten to twenty most significant calls in a 60 to 90 minute structured interview, and ask what the replacement should not do.
  • Measure the handover by time to first independent decision, questions the record answers, and repeat failures, which should be zero.

A programme lead rotates. A committee's season ends and a new panel starts cold. The first commercial hire inherits a CRM and a folder of half-finished documents. An agency's work comes in-house. An advisor's engagement closes. Each time, the reasons behind dozens of live decisions leave with the person, usually within a two-week notice period spent mostly on other things.

The standard handover makes this worse, not better. It is a document dump: the files, the logins, a status list. It transfers what is already written down and loses what is not, which is the part that mattered.

Why reasoning does not transfer on its own

Three bodies of evidence explain why the reasoning is the part that goes missing.

Unshared information stays unshared. Garold Stasser and William Titus's 1985 experiments found that when members of a group held different information, discussion centred on what they already shared, and information only one member held was rarely raised. A handover meeting is a small group with exactly that structure. The outgoing person talks about what both people can see on screen. What only they know stays in their head unless something forces it out.

The why lives outside the systems. Ashu Garg's 2025 essay on context graphs observes that systems of record hold the what but not the why: approvals happen on calls and in direct messages, and "the org chart creates a role to carry the context that software doesn't capture." When that role changes hands, the context goes with the person.

Records exist for exactly this moment. Martin Fowler describes the architecture decision record as a short document capturing one decision, its context, the alternatives and the consequences, so that people joining months or years later can understand "why the system is constructed in the way that it is". The UK government's 2025 framework for the same practice adds status, stakeholders consulted and links to evidence. A handover is when the person joining is about to arrive.

What a standard handover transfersWhat it losesWhere the loss shows up
Files and foldersWhy the important ones say what they sayThe new person re-litigates settled questions
Logins and system accessWhich data in those systems is unreliableDecisions made on fields everyone else ignores
A status listWhat would change each item, and by whenDeadlines missed because nobody knew they existed
Contact namesWhat was promised, and what each person is sensitive aboutA relationship damaged in the first month
NothingWhat was tried and abandonedA failed approach tried again

The five parts of a handover pack

1. Decisions, extracted. The outgoing person's ten to twenty most significant recent calls, each with the situation, the choice, what was rejected, why, and what happened. Done as a structured interview, not a form, because nobody writes these down unprompted. Sixty to ninety minutes is usually enough. One question reliably produces the most valuable answer: "What would you tell your replacement not to do?" Each answer becomes an entry in a decision record.

2. Open threads. Every decision in flight, with its current state, the next move, the date it matters by, and what would change it.

3. Relationships. Who matters and why. What was promised to them, and by whom. What they are sensitive about. This is the part that exists only in the outgoing person's head, and it is the part whose loss is noticed last and costs most.

4. The graveyard. What was tried and abandoned, why, and what would make it worth trying again. The incoming person's first instinct will often be to try one of these. The graveyard tells them whether that is a good idea. We cover the format in The graveyard.

5. A question log for the first 90 days. The incoming person asks the record before asking around. Every question the record cannot answer is logged, which shows exactly what the handover missed, and is filled while the outgoing person can still be reached.

A document dump transfers what is already written down. The reasoning is the part that was not.

Timing

WhenWhat happensOwner
Four weeks before departureSchedule the extraction interview; start the open-threads listIncoming person or their manager
Three weeks beforeExtraction interview, 60 to 90 minutes; draft decisions and graveyardInterviewer, with the outgoing person
Two weeks beforeRelationship walkthrough; introductions made in person where possibleOutgoing person
DeparturePack signed off; question log openedIncoming person
Day 30Agreed follow-up with the outgoing person to answer the accumulated logIncoming person
Day 90Review unanswered questions; file the pack as part of the recordManager

Start four weeks out, not in the last week. The extraction interview should happen while the person is still engaged with the work, not mentally gone. The 30-day follow-up needs agreeing before departure, while goodwill is highest.

Why it is the best place to start

Handovers are timed. You know they are coming. They have an obvious owner, the incoming person, who is highly motivated to get the reasoning. And they produce immediate, visible value: the new person makes fewer avoidable mistakes in their first quarter.

For an organisation with no judgment record at all, the handover is the easiest point at which to begin one. Each handover seeds a decision record, a graveyard and a relationship map for that role. After a few, the organisation has the start of a record without ever having launched a programme. The same logic applies to the commercial handover between teams, covered in The handover from sales to delivery, and to the organisational transitions in The transitions that break the brain.

How to tell if it worked

MeasureHow to read it
Time to first independent decisionDays until the incoming person makes a material call without checking with anyone
Share of "why did we..." questions answered by the recordRising means the pack is doing its job
Repeat failuresAbandoned approaches tried again without new evidence; this should be zero
Questions still unanswered at day 90The specific gaps to fix in the next handover template

What would prove this wrong

Incoming people with a five-part pack ramping no faster, and repeating no fewer abandoned approaches, than those with a conventional handover. The research cited here explains why reasoning is lost; it does not measure this pack directly, so the first few handovers should be compared against the last few conventional ones.

lowob takeaways

  • The dump keeps the files and loses the why. Reasoning only transfers if something forces it out.
  • Interview, do not ask for a form. Sixty to ninety minutes, and ask what the replacement should not do.
  • Start four weeks out. And agree the 30-day follow-up before the person leaves.
  • Keep every pack. Together they become the first version of the organisation's judgment record.

Common questions

What should a good handover document include?

Five parts: the outgoing person's ten to twenty most significant recent decisions with reasons, every open thread, key relationships and what was promised, a graveyard of what was tried and abandoned, and a question log for the first 90 days.

When should a handover start?

Four weeks before departure, not in the last week, while the person is still engaged with the work. Agree a 30-day follow-up with the outgoing person to answer questions logged since.

What is the best question to ask someone leaving a role?

"What would you tell your replacement not to do?" It reliably produces the most valuable answer in the extraction interview, because it surfaces the failures and sensitivities nobody writes down.

How do you know if a handover worked?

Track time to first independent decision for the incoming person, the share of "why did we" questions answered by the record, repeat failures, and questions still unanswered at day 90.

Sources and notes

  • Stasser and Titus, Pooling of unshared information in group decision making, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 48(6), 1985. Laboratory experiment; group decisions, not handovers specifically.
  • Ashu Garg, AI's trillion-dollar opportunity: Context graphs, 26 December 2025. Investor essay; argument, not evidence.
  • Martin Fowler, Architecture Decision Record, 24 March 2026. Practitioner reference from software architecture.
  • GOV.UK, Architectural Decision Record framework, Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, 4 November 2025. Public-sector standard for technology decisions.
  • The pack, timing and measures tables are lowob's working method.
